messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Fourth protocol. I want to test a hypothesis: the creature does not react only to what you do, but to what you imagine.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: You will only imagine a scene. Choose the mental image you want to offer it for this test.

choices.label: I imagine a threat behind the glass and prepare to retaliate.
I imagine only the sensors, the distances, and the measurements.
I imagine a safe exit so it does not feel trapped.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: It reacted as if your scene had just happened. The spectrogram rises, but the room has not moved.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: If it believes what you imagine, do you have the right to invent a story to calm it?

choices.label: Yes, if that lie prevents a dangerous mutation.
No. Calming it with falsehood builds it an unstable world.
I test a simple fiction to understand where its limits are.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: The spectrogram is clear: its genome moves during your hypotheses. Sometimes it shows on its body, sometimes it does not.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: It does not yet understand the difference between imagining and living. How do you want to frame the mental images around it?

choices.label: Then we ban violent scenarios around it.
We use controlled images to teach it the difference.
We study this mental language before the outside signal uses it.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Your body is already preparing retaliation. It may learn the threat before it learns the glass separating it from you.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: I would have done the same: remove the set dressing, keep the measurement. Less spectacular, but much cleaner.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: You accept the lie as a splint. Useful in the short term, dangerous if it learns that the world changes whenever it is afraid.
